Module 02 · Playbook

Playbook: from busy to productive

Diagnose, decide, block, execute, and review. Each step leaves an observable artifact.

Start
Practice
Observe one week, choose three priorities, protect focus blocks, and define evidence of progress.
Transfer
Repeat the system weekly and change one rule when evidence reveals recurring friction.
Journey outcomeDeliver a short activity log, three justified priorities, a protected calendar, and a review with decisions for the next week.
MasterclassWorkbookPlaybookPromptsAll resources
For teams

Make the work that deserves attention visible.

A full calendar does not prove progress. Without explicit criteria, urgent work displaces important work. Missing agreements also scatter team attention.

What you will gain

Leave with defensible priorities, protected time, and a simple way to review progress.

How to proceed

Diagnose, decide, block, execute, and review. Each step leaves an observable artifact.

What to verify

Deliver a short activity log, three justified priorities, a protected calendar, and a review with decisions for the next week.

Build my system

Repeat the system weekly and change one rule when evidence reveals recurring friction.

Starting point

Starting point

Turn a real week into a visible priority system: three justified outcomes, protected blocks, and a final review.

Diagnose, decide, block, execute, and review. Each step leaves an observable artifact.

  • Challenge

    Constant activity can hide a lack of progress. The challenge is to separate urgency, maintenance, and value-creating work before filling the calendar.

  • Practice

    Observe one week, choose three priorities, protect focus blocks, and define evidence of progress.

  • Evidence

    Deliver a short activity log, three justified priorities, a protected calendar, and a review with decisions for the next week.

Chapter 01

Governing principle

Principle: Value before volume

Productivity means completing results that serve an explicit purpose.

Decision it resolvesDefine the result first, then decide which activity deserves space.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. Write purpose and definition of done.
  2. Separate result, maintenance and coordination.
  3. Remove one activity that changes no decision.
  4. Name who approves the purpose and who reviews evidence.

Checklist

  • Result written.
  • Evidence defined.
  • Purpose approved and evidence assigned.
Decision rule
No task becomes a priority without a result and evidence. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Replace “answer email” with “resolve the three decisions blocking delivery”.
Antipattern
Using task count as proof of productivity.
Expected evidence
A defensible priority decision. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
Necessary maintenance may remain; its cost must stay visible. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

Chapter 02

Time log

Principle: Observe before optimizing

A time log reduces dependence on vague recollection of the week.

Decision it resolvesRecord facts for a sufficient period before redesigning.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. Capture start, end and output.
  2. Mark interruptions without judging them.
  3. Review gaps and doubtful data.
  4. Assign the record custodian and minimum read rights.

Checklist

  • Period identified.
  • Activities have outputs.
  • Record custody and permissions current.
Decision rule
A conclusion requires an inspectable record. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Record “10:00–10:35, meeting, output: date agreed”.
Antipattern
Backfilling the log to confirm a prior impression.
Expected evidence
Traceable time log. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
The log describes the observed period, not a universal rule. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

03
Chapter 03

Value map

Principle: Classify to decide

The value map separates creation, support, coordination and reaction.

Decision it resolvesKeep necessary work and question work that supports no result.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. Label each activity.
  2. Justify ambiguous cases.
  3. Total time only to describe, not promise impact.
  4. Agree with affected areas how ambiguous cases will be resolved.

Checklist

  • Categories complete.
  • Reasons concise.
  • Affected areas consulted on classification.
Decision rule
A category without a reason remains provisional. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Coordinating access is necessary support when it enables delivery.
Antipattern
Calling necessary but less visible obligations “noise”.
Expected evidence
Reviewable value map. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
Classification depends on purpose and may change with context. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

Chapter 04

Priority matrix

Principle: Compare with shared criteria

The matrix exposes impact, real urgency, effort, dependency and risk.

Decision it resolvesRank results with the same criteria and explain the trade-off.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. Define each criterion.
  2. Mark missing data.
  3. Review ties before deciding.
  4. Document the decision owner and dependency that may change it.

Checklist

  • Criteria defined.
  • Trade-off explicit.
  • Decision accountability and dependencies visible.
Decision rule
Scoring informs; the accountable person decides. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Two results tie: choose the one that clears a critical dependency.
Antipattern
Adding scores without explaining meaning or uncertainty.
Expected evidence
Three justified priorities. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
A matrix does not replace judgment, rights or existing commitments. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

Chapter 05

Work limit

Principle: Limit active fronts

A work limit exposes what is active and what is waiting.

Decision it resolvesFinish, pause or remove before opening another front.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. List active work.
  2. Set a small limit.
  3. Define exception and closure.
  4. Publish the active limit and who authorizes an exception.

Checklist

  • Limit published.
  • Queue visible.
  • Active limit and exception authority published.
Decision rule
Every active front has a next action or is paused. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Keep three weekly results active and an explicit queue.
Antipattern
Treating every request as started work.
Expected evidence
Fewer simultaneous fronts with clear status. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
The appropriate limit is contextual; no automatic outcome is promised. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

Chapter 06

Protected blocks

Principle: Reserve finished work

A protected block links priority, time and a concrete output.

Decision it resolvesSchedule only when inputs and a definition of done exist.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. Prepare input.
  2. Declare output.
  3. Reserve margin and review.
  4. Confirm inputs, block owner and output reviewer.

Checklist

  • Purpose visible.
  • Output bounded.
  • Inputs ready and output acceptance defined.
Decision rule
Redesign a block with no output before it starts. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: 09:00–10:30, produce a reviewable draft with five sources ready.
Antipattern
Filling the calendar without coordination or contingency capacity.
Expected evidence
Executable block. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
A legitimate, documented exception may reschedule a block. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

07
Chapter 07

Interruption protocol

Principle: Respond with a rule

The protocol avoids deciding every interruption from scratch.

Decision it resolvesChoose what to handle, delegate, batch, defer or discard.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. List frequent interruptions.
  2. Assign response and timing.
  3. Define who activates an exception.
  4. Assign each channel an owner and escalation path.

Checklist

  • Channels defined.
  • Responses agreed.
  • Channels, timing and escalation agreed.
Decision rule
Every exception records reason and next decision. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Non-urgent messages are batched; critical incidents use the agreed channel.
Antipattern
Blocking requests without a valid urgency path.
Expected evidence
Focus protection rules. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
The protocol does not remove surprises or replace response to real risks. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

08
Chapter 08

Weekly review

Principle: Review facts and rules

Weekly review connects results, deviations and adjustments.

Decision it resolvesKeep one useful rule and change one friction per cycle.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. Compare plan and execution.
  2. Explain one deviation with facts.
  3. Schedule the next review.
  4. Give the review to the sponsor with an adoption decision.

Checklist

  • Facts separated.
  • Decision written.
  • Sponsor informed and adoption gate decided.
Decision rule
Keep an improvement only while its evidence remains visible. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Keep prior preparation; adjust message rule; review Friday.
Antipattern
Turning review into blame or impressions.
Expected evidence
Testable weekly rule. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
One period is insufficient to claim general improvement. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

Chapter 09

Visible board

Principle: One view for decisions

The board combines priorities, blocks, status, evidence and next action.

Decision it resolvesShow only information that changes a decision.
Go deeperHow to apply it

How to apply it

  1. Publish three priorities.
  2. Update status and evidence.
  3. Remove unused fields.
  4. Configure board access by role and need.

Checklist

  • Current status.
  • Evidence linked.
  • Board access limited by need.
Decision rule
The board must be understandable without reconstructing conversations. Respect rights, sensitive data and shared commitments.
Example
Synthetic team example: Priority A: active; evidence: draft; next: review Thursday.
Antipattern
Building an ornamental board that costs more upkeep than the work.
Expected evidence
Visible weekly system. It is available for the agreed review.
Limit
Visibility must respect sensitive data and access rights. Do not scale without reviewing dependencies and adoption.

Glossary

Glossary

Result
Observable change or delivery with a definition of done.
Priority
Result chosen over explicit alternatives.
Protected block
Reserved time with purpose, output and boundary.
Dependency
External condition or contribution needed to continue.
Evidence
Observable record used to review a claim.
11
FAQ

Frequently asked questions

Always three priorities?

It is a practice limit that forces comparison; adjust it when context requires and document why. The sponsor documents any change to the limit.

What about a real urgency?

Use the defined exception, record its evidence and explicitly reschedule or remove work. The exception authority records the decision.

How do I know it improved?

Compare equivalent records and decide on one rule; do not turn one week into a general promise. The review team decides before scaling.

May I share the board?

Only with the rights and detail level agreed for the people involved. Permissions determine which detail may be shared.

  • Exceptions and backup ownership are defined.
  • Adoption is reviewed before scaling.
